title: S1 · Does EloValue show positive CLV when ROI is noisy?

hypothesis.statement: Bets placed when Elo disagrees with the closing market by at least θ beat the closing price by more than a random-bet control with the same fills, even though the ROI over the same bets cannot be distinguished from zero.
hypothesis.rationale: Closing prices are the sharpest estimate of true probability, so beating them is the cleanest evidence of edge; ROI over a few thousand bets at long odds has a confidence interval too wide to show it.
hypothesis.metric: CLV bootstrap 95% CI, random_bet control CLV, and ROI bootstrap 95% CI on the 2019+ holdout
hypothesis.threshold: Supported iff the CLV CI lies entirely above the control's CLV and the ROI CI contains 0.
hypothesis.in_sample: seasons <= 2018: pick θ from (0.02, 0.04, 0.06, 0.08, 0.1) with the highest CLV in excess of the control among grids with >= 300 bets
hypothesis.out_of_sample: seasons >= 2019, touched once, with the chosen θ

plain_title: Can a player-rating model spot mispriced odds?
plain_summary: We rate every player with Elo (a score that rises with wins and falls with losses) and bet whenever our rating likes a player clearly more than the bookmakers do. We then check whether those bets got better odds than the final pre-match odds, compared with simply betting at random. The better odds seen in the raw numbers turn out to come from the bookmaker we place bets with, not from the rating.
conclusion: EloValue's CLV does not exceed a random-bet control with the same fills: the positive raw CLV comes from the fill book's tighter prices, not from edge.
